title: You Learn This Too Late: Childhood Patterns Explained by Harvard & Stanford Expert
guest: Jane Marie Chen, co-founder of Embrace (low-cost infant incubators), author of the memoir Like a Wave We Break, leadership coach
summary: Jane Marie Chen, Harvard and Stanford alum whose company Embrace saved a million babies, discusses how childhood physical abuse in an immigrant family turned achievement into a coping mechanism that drove her to burnout and a breakdown when Embrace had to shut down. She explains how trauma lives in the body, why talk therapy failed her, and the practices that healed her: parts work, inner-child dialogue, confronting her parents for her own sake, boundaries with an open heart, the whole-body yes, and surrendering outcomes. The hosts connect this to high achievers who must untangle achievement from identity.

ideas.idea: Achievement is often a trauma response: people with perfect resumes frequently come from histories of trauma and achieve because they feel they are not enough.
ideas.detail: Chen sees this especially among entrepreneurs and social entrepreneurs; no number of degrees, accolades or babies saved could fill a void she could not articulate, which led her to burn out.

ideas.idea: When you rely on external validation the goalposts keep moving; everything you seek externally you have to find internally.
ideas.detail: Her overachiever part was protecting a very young part that never felt worthy; she spent most of her life wanting the world to prove her worth through achievements.

ideas.idea: Children of immigrants achieve to prove the family's sacrifice was worthwhile and to buy belonging and safety.
ideas.detail: Chen arrived in the US at four speaking no English, one of the only Asian families in her neighborhood; the hosts add that you feel you owe it to your ancestors to make the most of your life.

ideas.idea: Pressure from family sacrifice creates healthy drive until it tips into needing to prove, and you must become aware of which motivation is operating.
ideas.detail: Her mission with Embrace was healthy purpose and simultaneously a shadow side of proving she was OK; 'my pain became my purpose' had both sides at once.

ideas.idea: Cycles of abuse get normalized in Asian culture as cultural norms, and silence about them is complicity.
ideas.detail: She did not recognize being hit with a belt or slapped as abuse until her late 30s; a Taiwanese American friend from a violent home took his own life, which woke her up to speak out with her parents and community.

ideas.idea: Trauma is not left in the past; it rewires the brain and nervous system and is stored in the body and limbic system, so you cannot talk your way out of it, you have to feel your way through.
ideas.detail: Reading The Body Keeps the Score was a turning point; talk therapy never worked for her, and in business school she refused to discuss her childhood with a therapist.

ideas.idea: You cannot CEO your way through healing; instead of doing more, slow down and feel the heartbreak, fear and anger.
ideas.detail: After Embrace shut down she bought a one-way ticket to Indonesia with a surfboard and kept a spreadsheet of healing modalities, pivoting when one failed, before realizing the answer was stillness with the help of teachers, healers and friends. Jean says the fixer, A/B-testing product-manager mentality is exactly what she has to set down.

ideas.idea: Parts work (Internal Family Systems) means recognizing your overachiever, perfectionist, inner-critic parts as protectors and treating each with compassion rather than banishing them.
ideas.detail: Protector parts guard the parts carrying shame, rejection and abandonment; an ex nicknamed her warrior part Genghis Khan. She recommends the book No Bad Parts and a free parts-work exercise on her website.

ideas.idea: Say the words you wished a parent had said directly to your inner child; it only lands when it comes from yourself.
ideas.detail: At a van der Kolk psychodrama retreat she recruited a Santa-looking man and then a friend to play her ideal father reading scripted lines and felt nothing; reading the same lines to a photo of herself at five on her desk finally moved her.

ideas.idea: Peace with parents who hurt you comes from compassion for their whole history without condoning the behavior, holding boundaries and an open heart at the same time.
ideas.detail: Writing about how her parents grew up let her see how trauma seeps through lineages; she now tunes into bodily contraction around toxic behavior and chooses not to be around it, while carrying resentment would only hurt herself.

ideas.idea: Confronting your parents is not about changing them; it is about taking the hand of your inner child and standing up for her.
ideas.detail: Leadership coach Diana Chapman of the Conscious Leadership Group pushed her to have the conversation; she went in with no expectation her parents would change, and the outcome was learning to trust herself. The hosts extend this to partners and friends: speak your truth, and whether they absorb it is on them.

ideas.idea: Healthy boundaries with family make your yeses stronger and let you engage more wholeheartedly without underlying resentment.
ideas.detail: Raised as the holidays approach, since people who never learned boundaries growing up find them hardest to set with family.

ideas.idea: Use the 'whole body yes' test: when head, heart and gut align you feel a lifting line of energy; anything that does not feel that way deserves a pause and the question 'do I really want this?'
ideas.detail: On her book tour she was offered three events in one day in New York, felt contraction, and chose to do just one; for overachievers, the achievement is to not overachieve.

ideas.idea: Driving unhealthily hard lets you burn bright for a while and then burn out completely; sustainable impact requires daily self-care.
ideas.detail: When Embrace shut down after 10 years she had a full mental and physical breakdown that took a year and a half to recover from, and learned her mind was not invincible.

ideas.idea: What got you here will not get you to the next level; for high achievers the next level requires letting go rather than white-knuckled grinding.
ideas.detail: Cherie says a decade of teeth-clenched pushing ends in a breakdown, and growth now means surrender.

ideas.idea: Control is an illusion; give something your all and then surrender the outcome, and define success as living your values rather than external outcomes.
ideas.detail: The minute she stopped trying to control Embrace, Tony Robbins appeared out of nowhere and saved the company; she threw her single advance copy of her book into the ocean in Honolulu as a ceremony of releasing it to the universe.

ideas.idea: Over-optimizing every situation leaves no room for serendipity that may be beyond your imagination.
ideas.detail: Jean notes high achievers try to make everything as good as possible, but the best outcome may be something you could not have pictured, so some things must be out of your control.

ideas.idea: Success without fulfillment is the ultimate failure.
ideas.detail: Quoting Tony Robbins: many outwardly successful people are empty inside, always comparing to the next person as the goalposts move, so happiness stays an illusion.

ideas.idea: Self-compassion is a rubber coating around the glass ball of your identity so failures bounce rather than shatter you; you are worth more than the sum of your achievements.
ideas.detail: Cherie's image of untangling achievement from identity; Chen worries younger people let a post's like count destroy their sense of self.

ideas.idea: To feel again after years of numbness, sit in stillness and notice small physical sensations, since every emotion has a bodily correlate, and heal in community rather than isolation.
ideas.detail: 'We cannot heal what we cannot feel'; safe friends, therapists and teachers relax the nervous system enough to access emotions.

ideas.idea: Reaching the mission does not define you; the proudest achievement can be learning to embrace yourself.
ideas.detail: Embrace hit its goal of one million babies saved this year; Chen stepped down in May and now does corporate and individual leadership coaching teaching people to feel their feelings and step into alignment.
